tools.name: StoryMap on Well Infrastructure in CA
Drinking Water Tool – Your Water Data
Drinking Water Tool – CA Water Data

Existing Frameworks and Methods: No paper describes how a measurement becomes a management decision at the GSA level. Literature answers how you measure groundwater change but not necessarily what a measurement means for GSA decision making.
No real guidance on how to communicate uncertainty and differences in model selection.

§354.18(f) gives GSA the discretion to choose their won model and §351(h) requires using the best available science but doesn’t necessarily define a verification standarad for whether the science is applied correctly.
1.1 Land repurposing: Prospective / siting-only analysis, no paper documents a post-implementation verification approach for water savings or co-benefits for MLRP, stronger on siting and planning tools
No descriptions of financial models for securing long-term funding sustainability for monitoring, maitenance, and adaptive management (for post MLRP block grant expiration).

Dust emissions from fallowed and transitioning land noted as a serious potential harm, but no tracking or accounting protocols exists for measuring the co-harms or co-benefits of different multi-benefit land repurposing with regards to dust.

No specific measurement protocol for DAC health or equity outcomes that could be standardized across MLRP subbasins or incorporated into GSA reporting. (environmental health risk reduction indexes are directly related but more challenging to estimate and often constrained by limited geospatial data types and quality).
1.2 Ecological Co-benefits: No paper links co-benefit quantification to crediting system, and unresolved additionality and leakage concerns remain.
Statewide or regional studies and approaches don’t account for local ecosystem variability, and these co-benefit thresholds may need GSA specific calibration.
No monitoring network or dataset to support a threshold-based GDE accounting effort at a meaningful spatial scale—groundwater data available for only 1.3% of mapped GDE polygons statewide.
1.3 DAC Co-benefits: None of the outlined methods included DAC community input, affordability or well-owner level verification into the accounting frameworks.
No paper offers a well-failure or shortage-tracking method that doesn’t rely on undercounted self-reported data.
ISW: None of the reviewed literature has defined a crediting or accounting method, strictly summaries of modeling, quantifications and estimations

The analytical model methods described depend upon simplifying assumptions (steady-state conditions, linear aquifer response, uniform aquifer geometry) that quickly break down under real-world complexity. No real solution offered that could remain reliable under the transient, over-drafted of topographically complex conditions typical of managed CA basins.

No paper demonstrates the model outputs being operationalized into an actual SGMA compliant management decision. (Closing the loop) And no paper details method of communicating uncertainty quantification and error bounds.

Each method outlined requires data reliant on monitoring infrastructure that is not a given across CA GSAs. Motivates checking GSPs for calibrated regional models, dense well networks or historical gauge records.

Cumulative pumping problem is identified but not resolved in the reviewed papers (“total impact from multiple wells may not be equal to the sum of the effects of individual wells” (Zipper et al., 2018)

Disconnected or intermittent stream systems (common in CA over drafted basins) are not included in the reviewed analytical and statistical models. All depend on the assumption of hydraulic connectivity.

Land use and reacharge feedbacks explicitly excluded from optimization analyses—only pumping rates are changed and papers document opportunity to incorporate land use change in concert with adjusting pumping.
Recharge: AZ crediting infrastructure detailed but no peer reviewed documentation on CA SGMA aligned recharge crediting protocol. Are any GSA attempting an informal crediting without formal protocol?
No standardized method for parsing infiltration from actual recharge (may be remedied with vadose zone monitoring or multi-method comparison).
Spatial mismatch between recharge benefits and recovery (if recharge crediting done on a regional mass balance approach)

No literature tests whether CA GSAs recharge method choices are driven by data availability rather than hydrogoelogic suitabiltiy—Walker (2018) demonstrates in other settings available data is usually the key factor.
Cover Cropping: No peer-reviewed literature documents a formal process for estimating CUgw for cover cropping by incorporating accurate CUprecip

1.2 inch increase estimate from Islam et al. (2006) and the negligible ETa finding from DeVincentis et al. (2022) are slightly contradictory — requires a study that incorporates ET, drainage and soil moisture in CA conditions

Haven’t determined whether the CUprecip adjustment gap is something GSA have operationalized in GSP or if this is just a purely academic concern that has not run into with planning and implementation.
Demand Management: No supplied paper gives a California SGMA parcel-level crediting protocol for fallowing, efficiency, or crop-switching actions in methods/results detail.
No supplied paper describes water-transfer accounting or temporary water-right transaction verification in a groundwater management program.

Most papers depend on multi-decade metered pumping data which Kansas has, but most CA GSAs do not, signaling a data infrastructure gap for CA. The causal impact and regression methods are sound but not transferable withtout the data foundation.
Floodplain Connection & Flood Control: No formal description of how to credit flood-MAR recharge volumes to specific land parcels or landowners, most work focuses on the measurement methods.
No reliable method addressed for converting measured infiltration or inundation extent into confirmed aquifer recharge.
None of the papers fully address the flood control co-benefits — flood risk reduction, habitat, etc.
Missing the relationship between land use change and repurposing and floodplain connection.

No reliable field-scale method for measuring the parameter the papers find most influential (clogging-layer conductance and specific yield). This leaves flood-MAR recharge estimates dependent on values neither paper can measure with real confidence.
